primary.title: Unverified Claim That Robert Maxwell Aided Mogilevich's Passport and Banking Network
primary.description_short: Unverified TrumpFile allegation that Robert Maxwell helped Mogilevich obtain passports and banking access.
primary.description_medium: TrumpFile’s timeline alleges that Robert Maxwell arranged Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates in 1988, opened a Bank of New York account used for laundering, and connected Mogilevich with KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov. An FBI report dated August 1996 instead names Shabtai Kalmanovich in connection with passport access. Neither source independently establishes Maxwell’s alleged role or a relationship to Donald Trump.
primary.description_long: TrumpFile labels this account “Robert Maxwell obtains passports for Mogilevich, helps KGB” and dates its timeline item July 1, 1988. The page’s narrative says the alleged passport arrangement happened “sometime in 1988,” and alleges that Maxwell obtained Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates, set up a Bank of New York account for money laundering, and introduced Mogilevich to KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov. These are claims made by TrumpFile, not independently verified findings. A separately accessed text extraction of an FBI report dated August 1996 says Israeli passports had been obtained by Shabtai Kalmanovich for members of organized-crime groups including the Mogilevich organization. That report does not establish Maxwell’s alleged role, the Bank of New York account, or the KGB connection; its reference to Kalmanovich also cautions against treating TrumpFile’s attribution as confirmed. No passport, bank, court, or contemporaneous record confirming Maxwell’s role is supplied. The packet also provides no link between this 1988 allegation and Donald Trump. This internal draft preserves what the supplied timeline alleges while leaving its date at year-level precision and marking the event unverified; the exact day, related outcomes, and asserted Trump relevance remain unresolved.

frozen_original.title: Trump Withdraws from Paris Climate Agreement Again on Day One
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed an executive order withdrawing the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement for the second time, having previously withdrawn in 2017 and rejoined under Biden. The immediate withdrawal signaled to the world that U.S. climate commitments were fundamentally unreliable, undermining international negotiations and emboldening other nations to weaken their own pledges. Scientists and foreign leaders expressed alarm that the world's second-largest carbon emitter was again abdicating its responsibilities at a moment when climate action was more urgent than ever. The move was celebrated by fossil fuel executives who attended Trump's inauguration.

frozen_original.title: Trump Organization Loans to Trump at Favorable Rates — Tax Manipulation Scheme
frozen_original.synopsis: Prior to his presidency, Trump engaged in complex financial transactions with the Trump Organization in which loans to himself at artificially favorable interest rates were used to shift income and minimize tax liability. The New York Attorney General's investigation and subsequent civil fraud lawsuit revealed a pattern of asset valuation manipulation for tax and lending purposes. Trump properties were valued higher when seeking loans from banks and lower when calculating taxes. A New York court found Trump liable for fraud, ordered him to pay $364 million in penalties, and barred him from serving as an officer of New York corporations.

primary.title: New York judge finds Trump defendants used false financial data to secure lower loan rates
primary.description_short: A 2024 New York civil ruling found false financial statements were used to obtain financing on more favorable terms.
primary.description_medium: In a February 2024 civil fraud ruling, a New York judge found that Trump and related defendants submitted false financial data to obtain financing on more favorable terms. The decision concerns statements and lending terms for entity borrowing. It does not establish that the Trump Organization lent money to Trump personally or that a loan scheme shifted his taxable income.
primary.description_long: This repair is limited to the February 2024 New York Supreme Court decision in the state’s civil fraud case. After a nonjury trial, Justice Arthur Engoron found the defendants liable and wrote that they had submitted false financial data to obtain borrowing at lower rates. The decision describes Trump-controlled entities borrowing from banks and other lenders, with lenders requiring personal guarantees from Trump based on statements of financial condition. The source-supported event is the court’s finding about financial statements and lending terms. It is not a finding that the Trump Organization loaned money to Trump personally at artificially favorable rates, and the sources reviewed do not establish that such loans shifted income or minimized tax liability. Those distinct assertions from the frozen entry are excluded from this card. The corrected date identifies the 2024 ruling, rather than treating 2012 as the date of the court finding. The record does not state a measured public loss, so none is inferred here.

frozen_original.title: Trump signs order allowing indefinite detention without charge for immigrants
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed an executive order authorizing the indefinite detention of immigrants without filing charges, violating due process protections and fundamental constitutional rights. The order directed immigration judges to deny bail hearings and allowed ICE to hold individuals indefinitely while immigration courts remained backlogged. Federal judges immediately moved to block the order, ruling that even non-citizens have due process rights under the Fifth Amendment. The order was part of a systematic effort to eliminate judicial oversight of immigration enforcement.

primary.title: Trump Order Calls for Immigration Detention Pending Proceedings, Subject to Law
primary.description_short: Trump's Jan. 20 order directs detention of removable immigrants pending proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law.
primary.description_medium: Section 10 of the Jan. 20, 2025 order directs DHS to use or establish detention facilities and to detain people apprehended for immigration-law violations pending removal proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law. That text supports a detention directive; it does not itself establish indefinite detention without charge, denied bail hearings, or immediate court blocks.
primary.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” Section 10 directs the Homeland Security secretary to take appropriate action and use legally available resources or contracts for facilities to detain removable immigrants. It further directs detention of people apprehended for immigration-law violations while removal proceedings are pending or until removal, “to the extent permitted by law.” The order therefore supports describing a federal detention directive tied to removal proceedings and an express legal limitation. The text does not itself say that immigrants may be held indefinitely without charges, instruct immigration judges to deny bail hearings, or report that federal judges immediately blocked the order. The supplied card made those additional claims without providing a court ruling or other supporting source; they are omitted here. The order’s language alone also does not establish how long anyone was detained, how many people were affected, what agencies implemented, or how a court later ruled. This corrected entry records what the signed order says without turning its detention language into unsupported claims about custody duration, court action, or a legal finding.

corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” Section 10 directs the Homeland Security secretary to take appropriate action and use legally available resources or contracts for facilities to detain removable immigrants. It further directs detention of people apprehended for immigration-law violations while removal proceedings are pending or until removal, “to the extent permitted by law.” The order therefore supports describing a federal detention directive tied to removal proceedings and an express legal limitation. The text does not itself say that immigrants may be held indefinitely without charges, instruct immigration judges to deny bail hearings, or report that federal judges immediately blocked the order. The supplied card made those additional claims without providing a court ruling or other supporting source; they are omitted here. The order’s language alone also does not establish how long anyone was detained, how many people were affected, what agencies implemented, or how a court later ruled. This corrected entry records what the signed order says without turning its detention language into unsupported claims about custody duration, court action, or a legal finding.

source_fact_map.fact: Section 10 directs detention of people apprehended for immigration-law violations while removal proceedings or removal are pending, to the extent permitted by law.
source_fact_map.quote: pending the outcome of their removal proceedings or their removal from the country, to the extent permitted by law
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Sec. 10. Detention Facilities. The Secretary of Homeland Security shall promptly take all appropriate action and allocate all legally available resources or establish contracts to construct, operate, control, or use facilities to detain removable aliens. The Secretary of Homeland Security, further, shall take all appropriate actions to ensure the detention of aliens apprehended for violations of immigration law pending the outcome of their removal proceedings or their removal from the country, to the extent permitted by law.
